title: Gastrointestinal Blood Supply
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows blood into, through, and out of the gut. It covers the three unpaired aortic branches and their territories, the watershed zones of the colon, the portal venous system and the escape routes portal blood takes when the liver obstructs it, the two territories of the anal canal, and the dual inflow of the liver. Board questions usually give a bleeding ulcer, a hypotensive episode, a sign on the abdominal wall, or an enlarged groin node and ask for the vessel, segment, or drainage path responsible. If you know which embryonic gut segment each organ comes from and that portal blood must cross a second capillary bed in the liver, most of these questions can be reasoned out.
prerequisites: Foregut, midgut, and hindgut divisions and their derivatives (GI-1)
Peritoneal relations: hepatoduodenal ligament, lesser sac, and retroperitoneal organs (GI-4)
Liver lobule, acinus, and sinusoid histology (GI-2)
Pressure, flow, and resistance relationships and Starling forces in capillaries

connections.how: Cirrhosis is the usual cause of portal hypertension, and its complications (varices, splenomegaly, ascites, encephalopathy) follow from the venous anatomy in this chapter.
Acute and chronic mesenteric ischemia, ischemic colitis, and variceal bleeding are applications of the arterial territories and anastomoses taught here.
The site of a peptic ulcer predicts whether it bleeds from a named artery or perforates into the peritoneal cavity.
Venous drainage explains why gut cancers metastasize first to the liver, and lymph drainage across the pectinate line predicts nodal spread of anal cancers.
Shock, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation emboli injure the gut and liver through the same flow, pressure, and watershed principles that apply in other organs.

terms.def: A region at the border between two arterial territories, supplied by the most distal branches of each, where perfusion pressure is lowest during a global fall in flow.
A continuous arterial channel along the mesenteric border of the colon formed by anastomoses between the colic branches of the SMA and IMA.
A venous arrangement in which blood passes through two capillary beds in series; the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the gut capillaries to the liver sinusoids.
A wide, fenestrated hepatic capillary without a continuous basement membrane, where portal and arterial blood mix and exchange with hepatocytes across the space of Disse.
Abnormally high pressure in the portal venous system, caused by increased resistance to flow before, within, or after the liver.
The difference between wedged (sinusoidal) and free hepatic venous pressure; normally about 1 to 5 mmHg.
A site where a tributary of the portal vein communicates with a systemic vein, providing a bypass around the liver when portal pressure rises.
A dilated, tortuous vein; in portal hypertension, thin-walled submucosal veins at portosystemic anastomoses enlarge into varices.
Dilated superficial abdominal wall veins radiating from the umbilicus, fed by paraumbilical veins in portal hypertension.
The serrated line formed by the bases of the anal valves, marking the junction of hindgut endoderm above and proctodeal ectoderm below.
Dilation of hepatic arterioles when portal flow falls, mediated by accumulation of adenosine that portal flow normally washes away.
The capillary network around the intrahepatic bile ducts, supplied by branches of the hepatic artery.

sections.title: The celiac trunk and its branches

blocks.text: Three unpaired arteries leave the front of the abdominal aorta to supply the gut, and each serves one embryonic segment. The celiac trunk arises at about T12, just below the aortic hiatus, and supplies the foregut derivatives: the abdominal esophagus, stomach, duodenum to the major papilla, liver, gallbladder, and much of the pancreas. The spleen, which develops in the dorsal mesogastrium, is supplied by the same trunk. After a short course the trunk divides into three branches.

blocks.title: Branches of the celiac trunk
rows: Up to the esophagogastric junction, then along the lesser curvature
Tortuous, along the upper border of the pancreas, behind the stomach
Pancreatic branches, short gastrics, left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic)
Body and tail of pancreas, fundus, upper greater curvature, spleen
To the right, then divides near the duodenum
Proper hepatic (right and left hepatic, usually right gastric) and gastroduodenal
Liver, gallbladder (cystic artery, usually from right hepatic), pylorus, lesser curvature
Descends behind the first part of the duodenum
First part of duodenum, pancreatic head, lower greater curvature
blocks.caption: Each curvature of the stomach carries a pair of arteries that anastomose: left and right gastric along the lesser curvature, left and right gastro-omental along the greater.

blocks.text: Because the stomach receives arteries from every celiac branch and these join along both curvatures, gastric infarction is rare. The splenic artery, by contrast, divides into segmental branches within the spleen that behave as end arteries, so emboli produce wedge-shaped splenic infarcts. The superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the gastroduodenal artery anastomose around the pancreatic head with the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery from the SMA. This arcade marks the foregut to midgut boundary and is the main collateral between the celiac and SMA territories, so slow narrowing of one origin can be bypassed through the other.
Ulcer location predicts the bleeding vessel

A peptic ulcer erodes whatever lies beneath it. The gastroduodenal artery runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum, so a posterior duodenal bulb ulcer can open it and cause brisk hematemesis or melena with hemodynamic instability. A lesser curvature gastric ulcer can erode the left gastric artery. An anterior duodenal ulcer has no large artery behind it, and its base faces the free peritoneal cavity, so it is more likely to perforate, releasing gas that collects under the diaphragm on an upright radiograph and causing chemical then bacterial peritonitis.

blocks.predict: A patient with a posterior duodenal bulb ulcer and another with an anterior duodenal ulcer both deteriorate suddenly. Which is more likely to show free air under the diaphragm, and which a falling hemoglobin?
blocks.explain: The anterior ulcer perforates into the peritoneal cavity, so gas escapes and rises under the diaphragm. The posterior ulcer sits on the gastroduodenal artery and erodes it, so it bleeds into the lumen and the hemoglobin falls.
blocks.check: The paragraph on ulcer location and the course of the gastroduodenal artery in the table.

sections.title: Mesenteric arteries, the marginal artery, and watershed ischemia

blocks.text: The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) arises at about L1, passes behind the neck of the pancreas and in front of the third part of the duodenum, and supplies the midgut: the duodenum below the major papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and proximal two thirds of the transverse colon. The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) arises at about L3 and supplies the hindgut: the distal third of the transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, and upper rectum.

blocks.title: Mesenteric artery territories
rows: Inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal and ileal, ileocolic, right colic, middle colic
Distal duodenum to proximal two thirds of transverse colon
Distal third of transverse colon to upper rectum
Middle rectal; inferior rectal via internal pudendal
blocks.caption: The rectum has three arterial sources, which is why it is usually spared in low-flow ischemia.

blocks.text: Branches of the colic arteries join near the mesenteric border of the colon to form the marginal artery, a continuous channel from the ileocolic region to the rectosigmoid. It links the SMA and IMA, so a slowly occluding IMA (as in atherosclerosis) can be bypassed. The link is weakest at two points. At the splenic flexure, the terminal branches of the middle colic (SMA) and left colic (IMA) meet, and the marginal artery there is thin or sometimes discontinuous. At the rectosigmoid junction, the last sigmoid artery meets the superior rectal artery with few connecting vessels.

These watershed zones sit at the far end of two territories, so pressure has already fallen along each supply before reaching them. When systemic pressure or cardiac output falls, as in shock, heart failure, dehydration, or after major surgery, they are the first to lose adequate flow. The mucosa is injured first because it has the highest metabolic demand and lies at the end of the penetrating vessels. Ischemic colitis typically presents in an older patient with sudden cramping left-sided abdominal pain followed within about a day by bloody diarrhea, because sloughing mucosa bleeds. Imaging may show thumbprinting, the rounded indentations produced by submucosal edema and hemorrhage. Most cases are nonocclusive and confined to the mucosa; transmural infarction leads to perforation and peritonitis.

blocks.title: From hypotension to ischemic colitis
steps: Cardiac output or systemic pressure falls
Mesenteric vasoconstriction diverts flow to heart and brain
Watershed zones receive the least perfusion pressure
Mucosa, with the highest demand, becomes ischemic first
Mucosal necrosis and sloughing
Cramping pain, then bloody diarrhea
blocks.caption: Splenic flexure and rectosigmoid are affected first; the rectum is spared by its dual supply.

blocks.text: Ischemic colitis differs from acute mesenteric ischemia of the small bowel. An embolus from the left atrium in atrial fibrillation enters the SMA because it leaves the aorta at an acute angle, and it often lodges near the origin of the middle colic artery. Visceral pain fibers sense ischemia while the parietal peritoneum is not yet involved, so pain is severe but the abdomen is soft: pain out of proportion to the examination. Lactate rises as the bowel shifts to anaerobic metabolism. Chronic narrowing of two or more mesenteric origins produces postprandial pain (intestinal angina), because digestion demands a rise in flow the narrowed vessels cannot deliver, so patients fear food and lose weight.

sections.title: The portal venous pathway through the liver

blocks.text: Venous blood from the abdominal gut, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder does not go straight to the inferior vena cava (IVC). It collects in the hepatic portal vein and passes through a second capillary bed, the liver sinusoids, before returning to the heart. Absorbed nutrients, drugs, hormones such as insulin and glucagon, and bacterial products therefore reach hepatocytes first, which allows first-pass metabolism, nutrient storage, and clearance of gut-derived toxins such as ammonia and endotoxin.

The superior mesenteric vein (SMV) and splenic vein join behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein. The inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein, though it may enter the SMV or the confluence. The portal vein passes behind the first part of the duodenum and ascends in the free edge of the hepatoduodenal ligament, where it lies posterior to the common bile duct (on the right) and the proper hepatic artery (on the left). Along the way it receives the left and right gastric veins, and the cystic and paraumbilical veins drain into it or its branches. At the porta hepatis it divides into right and left branches that follow the arteries and bile ducts into the portal tracts.

blocks.title: Path of portal blood
steps: SMV and splenic vein join behind the pancreatic neck
Portal vein ascends in the hepatoduodenal ligament
Right and left branches to portal tract venules
Mixes with hepatic arterial blood in sinusoids
Central veins collect sinusoidal blood
Sublobular veins to right, middle, and left hepatic veins
Hepatic veins enter the IVC below the diaphragm
blocks.caption: Blood flows from the portal tract (zone 1) toward the central vein (zone 3), while bile flows the opposite way toward the portal tract.

blocks.text: The sinusoids are fenestrated and lack a continuous basement membrane, so plasma reaches hepatocyte microvilli in the space of Disse. Because blood enters at the portal tract and leaves at the central vein, hepatocytes in zone 3 (around the central vein) receive the least oxygen. They are the first to die in shock and the first to congest when hepatic venous pressure rises in right heart failure, producing the nutmeg liver.

Normal portal pressure is low, about 5 to 10 mmHg, and hepatic venous pressure is near 0 mmHg, so the liver offers little resistance. The portal system has essentially no valves, so any rise in resistance between the gut and the right atrium raises pressure throughout it. Classifying the obstruction by its site explains the findings.

blocks.title: Causes of portal hypertension by site
rows: Wedged hepatic pressure may be normal
Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis), right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis
blocks.caption: HVPG above about 5 mmHg defines sinusoidal portal hypertension; above about 10 mmHg it is clinically significant.

blocks.text: As portal pressure rises, splenic venous outflow is impeded, so the spleen congests and enlarges, which sequesters platelets (hypersplenism). Raised sinusoidal pressure drives fluid into the space of Disse faster than hepatic lymphatics can remove it, which contributes to ascites.

At a few sites, small tributaries of the portal vein and of systemic veins drain the same tissue and connect with each other. In health these connections carry little blood, because portal pressure is only slightly higher than systemic venous pressure. When portal pressure rises, blood flows down the new gradient from the portal side into the systemic side, and the thin connecting veins dilate. The same shunting lets gut blood bypass hepatocytes, so ammonia and other gut-derived compounds reach the brain and contribute to hepatic encephalopathy.

blocks.title: Portosystemic anastomoses
rows: Esophageal veins draining to the azygos and hemiazygos veins
Paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament
Superficial and deep epigastric and thoracoepigastric veins
Middle and inferior rectal veins draining to the internal iliac veins
Lumbar, renal, and other retroperitoneal veins
blocks.caption: The first three sites are the classic examination triad: top, middle, and bottom of the abdominal gut.

blocks.text: Esophageal varices are the most dangerous. They lie in the submucosa of the lower esophagus with little surrounding tissue support. By the law of Laplace, wall stress equals pressure times radius divided by wall thickness, so as a varix widens and its wall thins, stress rises until the wall ruptures; the risk is substantial once HVPG exceeds about 12 mmHg. Bleeding is brisk because the vein carries portal pressure.

blocks.title: From cirrhosis to variceal hemorrhage
steps: Fibrosis and sinusoidal narrowing raise intrahepatic resistance
Portal pressure rises; HVPG above about 10 mmHg
Left gastric vein flow reverses toward the esophagus
Submucosal esophageal veins dilate into varices
Wall stress rises as radius grows and wall thins
Rupture causes massive hematemesis
blocks.caption: Coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia from liver disease and hypersplenism worsen the bleed.

blocks.text: The paraumbilical veins accompany the ligamentum teres in the falciform ligament from the left portal vein to the umbilicus. Portal blood reaching them flows into abdominal wall veins and radiates outward from the navel as caput medusae: upward above the umbilicus and downward below it. In IVC obstruction, by contrast, leg blood returns to the heart through abdominal wall veins, so flow below the umbilicus runs upward. Anorectal varices form where the superior rectal vein meets the middle and inferior rectal veins. They are not the same as hemorrhoids, which are enlarged anal vascular cushions caused mainly by straining and raised abdominal pressure rather than by portal hypertension.

blocks.predict: Dilated abdominal wall veins are seen in one patient with cirrhosis and in another with IVC obstruction. How would emptying a vein below the umbilicus and watching it refill tell them apart?
blocks.explain: In portal hypertension blood radiates away from the umbilicus, so veins below it fill from above and flow downward. In IVC obstruction, blood from the legs must return to the heart through the abdominal wall, so veins below the umbilicus flow upward, often along the flanks.
blocks.check: The caput medusae paragraph and the umbilical row of the table.

blocks.title: Gastric varices with a normal liver
blocks.text: A patient with chronic pancreatitis vomits blood. Endoscopy shows large varices in the gastric fundus but none in the esophagus, and liver tests are normal. Inflammation in the pancreatic bed has thrombosed the splenic vein, which runs along the back of the pancreas. Splenic blood reroutes through the short gastric veins into the submucosal veins of the fundus, which dilate, and then reaches the portal vein through the gastric veins. Portal pressure itself is normal, so the esophageal anastomosis is not stressed. This is sinistral (left-sided) portal hypertension, a prehepatic cause, and the spleen is congested and enlarged.

sections.title: The anal canal above and below the pectinate line

blocks.text: The pectinate (dentate) line is formed by the bases of the anal valves about midway along the anal canal. It marks the site of the embryonic anal membrane, where the endoderm of the hindgut (cloaca) met the ectoderm of the proctodeum. Tissue above the line therefore behaves like gut and tissue below it like skin, and every feature follows from that origin.

blocks.title: Anal canal by the pectinate line
rows: Simple columnar, with a narrow transitional zone near the line
Stratified squamous nonkeratinized, becoming keratinized skin at the anal verge
Inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal, internal iliac)
Superior rectal vein to IMV to portal vein
Inferior rectal vein to internal pudendal and internal iliac veins to IVC (systemic)
Internal iliac nodes (upper canal also along superior rectal vessels to inferior mesenteric nodes)
Visceral afferents with the inferior hypogastric plexus
Somatic inferior rectal nerves (branches of the pudendal nerve, S2 to S4)
Senses stretch only; painless to cutting or pinching
Sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature
External hemorrhoids (painful when thrombosed); fissures; squamous cell carcinoma
blocks.caption: The middle rectal arteries and veins (internal iliac) also supply and drain the region around the anorectal junction.

blocks.text: Pain is the clearest clinical consequence. Visceral afferents above the line respond to distension but not to cutting, so internal hemorrhoids, polyps, and early tumors there are painless, and bright red blood on the stool may be the only sign. Below the line, the inferior rectal nerves carry somatic sensation, so a thrombosed external hemorrhoid or an anal fissure (a tear in the squamous lining, usually in the posterior midline) causes sharp, well-localized pain, especially on defecation.

Drainage predicts spread. Venous blood above the line enters the portal system, so adenocarcinoma of the rectum and upper canal can metastasize to the liver, while blood below the line enters the IVC and reaches the lungs first. Lymph from below the line goes to the superficial inguinal nodes, which can be felt in the groin, whereas nodes draining the upper canal lie deep in the pelvis and are not palpable. Squamous cell carcinoma, which arises from the squamous and transitional epithelium and is strongly associated with human papillomavirus, therefore often presents with an enlarged inguinal node.

blocks.title: Localizing an anal lesion
blocks.text: A patient reports painful defecation, a firm mass at the anal verge, and a hard, enlarged node in the groin. Pain means somatic innervation, so the lesion is below the pectinate line. Squamous epithelium lines that region, so the likely cancer is squamous cell carcinoma, and its lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, explaining the palpable node. A second patient has painless bright red bleeding and a mass felt above the line on digital examination. Visceral innervation explains the absent pain, the columnar lining predicts adenocarcinoma, nodal spread goes to pelvic nodes that cannot be felt, and venous spread through the superior rectal vein goes to the liver.

sections.title: Dual blood supply of the liver

blocks.text: The liver receives about 1350 mL of blood per minute, roughly a quarter of resting cardiac output. About 75% arrives through the portal vein at low pressure and about 25% through the hepatic artery at systemic arterial pressure. Portal blood has already passed through the gut and spleen and is partly deoxygenated, but its larger volume means each inflow delivers roughly half of the oxygen the liver uses. Both streams enter the same sinusoids from the portal tracts, so every hepatocyte is perfused by both.

The liver cannot control portal inflow, which is set by the splanchnic arterioles upstream in the gut and spleen. It does control hepatic arterial inflow, and it uses this to buffer changes in portal flow.

blocks.title: Hepatic arterial buffer response
steps: Portal flow falls
Less adenosine is washed from around hepatic arterioles
Adenosine accumulates and dilates the arterioles
Hepatic arterial flow rises
Total flow and adenosine washout partly recover
blocks.caption: The response works in one direction only: arterial flow compensates for portal changes, but portal flow does not compensate for arterial changes.

blocks.text: These features explain why hepatic infarction is uncommon. Occluding a portal vein branch usually causes only a sharply outlined red zone of sinusoidal congestion and hepatocyte atrophy without necrosis (the infarct of Zahn, which is not a true infarct). Ligating the common hepatic artery proximal to the gastroduodenal artery is usually tolerated, because blood from the SMA reaches the proper hepatic artery backward through the pancreaticoduodenal arcades and gastroduodenal artery (C01). True infarction needs loss of arterial flow together with poor portal flow or absent collaterals.

Global hypoperfusion is a different problem. In shock or severe heart failure both inflows fall together, and the zone 3 hepatocytes at the end of the sinusoid die first. This ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) produces a sharp rise in aminotransferases, often above 1000 U/L, that falls quickly once perfusion is restored.

The bile ducts have no such backup. Their peribiliary vascular plexus is supplied only by branches of the hepatic artery, so hepatocytes may survive arterial occlusion while ducts do not. After liver transplantation, the graft has no arterial collaterals, and hepatic artery thrombosis causes ischemic cholangiopathy: duct necrosis, bile leaks, strictures, and cholangitis. A similar arterial preference explains imaging of hepatocellular carcinoma, which draws its blood mainly from the hepatic artery, so it enhances brightly in the arterial phase and appears to wash out in the portal venous phase.

blocks.predict: After liver transplantation, one patient develops portal vein thrombosis and another hepatic artery thrombosis. Which is more likely to develop bile duct strictures, and why?
blocks.explain: Hepatic artery thrombosis. The peribiliary plexus depends on hepatic arterial blood alone, and the graft has no collaterals, so the ducts become ischemic. Portal vein thrombosis reduces hepatocyte inflow, but the hepatic arterial buffer response raises arterial flow and the ducts keep their supply.
blocks.check: The buffer response cycle and the bile duct paragraph.

integration.text: Embryology organizes the anatomy. The foregut, midgut, and hindgut each take one unpaired aortic branch, their borders are where collateral arcades and watershed zones form, and the junction of endoderm and ectoderm at the pectinate line divides the anal canal into a gut-like and a skin-like territory with separate vessels, nodes, and nerves. Physiology supplies the mechanisms: watershed zones fail first because pressure has fallen by the time blood reaches them, mucosa is injured first because its demand is highest, and the liver protects its hepatocytes through two inflows and the adenosine-driven buffer response while leaving the bile ducts dependent on the artery alone.

Pathology and microbiology apply the same map. Cirrhosis from alcohol, viral hepatitis, or fatty liver disease raises sinusoidal resistance, schistosome eggs block presinusoidal venules, and pancreatitis thromboses the splenic vein, and each produces a predictable pattern of varices and splenomegaly. Venous drainage explains why colorectal cancer seeds the liver, and lymph drainage explains which nodes an anal cancer reaches. Arterial branching and collateral capacity vary between individuals, so these rules predict the typical case.

summary: The celiac trunk (about T12), SMA (about L1), and IMA (about L3) supply the foregut, midgut, and hindgut, with the spleen supplied by the celiac trunk.
A posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery and bleeds; a lesser curvature gastric ulcer erodes the left gastric artery; an anterior duodenal ulcer tends to perforate.
The marginal artery links SMA and IMA, but it is weakest at the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction, which are the first sites of ischemic colitis after hypotension.
The SMV and splenic vein form the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck; portal blood passes through sinusoids to central veins, hepatic veins, and the IVC.
Portal hypertension is classified as prehepatic, intrahepatic (presinusoidal or sinusoidal), or posthepatic, and cirrhosis is the most common cause.
The portosystemic anastomoses at the esophagus, umbilicus, and rectum produce esophageal varices, caput medusae, and anorectal varices.
Above the pectinate line the canal is columnar, portal-drained, internal iliac node-drained, and painless; below it is squamous, systemically drained, inguinal node-drained, and painful.
The liver receives about 75% of its blood from the portal vein and about 25% from the hepatic artery, each providing about half its oxygen, so infarction is uncommon.
The hepatic arterial buffer response raises arterial inflow when portal flow falls, through local adenosine accumulation.
The bile ducts depend on the hepatic artery alone, so hepatic artery thrombosis after transplantation causes ischemic cholangiopathy and strictures.

verify: Vertebral levels for the celiac trunk (T12 or T12 to L1), SMA (L1), and IMA (L3) vary slightly between anatomy texts; confirm the values NABNE expects.
Normal portal pressure is quoted as about 5 to 10 mmHg in different sources (Guyton and Hall gives about 9 mmHg); HVPG thresholds of above 5, 10, and 12 mmHg follow current hepatology consensus.
The split of hepatic blood flow (about 75% portal, 25% arterial) and of oxygen delivery (about half each) varies slightly between physiology texts.
The eponyms Griffiths point (splenic flexure), Sudeck point (rectosigmoid), marginal artery of Drummond, and infarct of Zahn are omitted or used sparingly; confirm whether NABNE expects them.
Variant hepatic arteries (replaced right hepatic from the SMA, replaced left hepatic from the left gastric) are common but not covered here; confirm whether they are tested.
Pectinate line position (about midway along the anal canal, or at the junction of its upper two thirds and lower third) differs between texts.
Typical SMA embolus lodging site (at or just beyond the middle colic origin) is quoted with slight variation between sources.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: gut-arteries (aorta with celiac, SMA, and IMA branches and watershed zones), portal-anastomoses (portal system with the three classic portosystemic sites), and pectinate-line (anal canal cross-section with supply above and below the line).
